profane

pruh-FAYN -- from Latin pro- ('outside') plus fanum ('temple'): to drag something out of the temple and treat it as ordinary. · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To profane is to treat something sacred with great disrespect.

The soldiers who stabled their horses inside the cathedral did more than trespass; they profaned it.

Example

Desperate for a dramatic shot, a film crew profanes a temple where worshippers have knelt in silence for six hundred years, setting up floodlights and shouting orders through its halls.

The crew profanes the temple by treating what others hold sacred as though it were ordinary property. Unlike 'damage,' which requires physical harm, you can profane a place without leaving a single scratch.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

defile: To defile is to spoil the purity of something -- mud tracked over a white gown, graffiti across a fresh monument. To profane aims at the sacred specifically: it treats a holy place, object, or ritual as though it were ordinary. You can defile anything clean; you profane only what is sacred.

dishonor: To dishonor is to bring shame on someone or something -- a family name, a uniform, a promise. To profane is narrower and sharper: it treats what people hold sacred as though it were worthless. Breaking your word dishonors you; treating a shrine like a storage shed profanes it.

violate: To violate is to break or fail to respect something -- a rule, a border, a person's privacy. To profane always points at the sacred: a treaty can be violated, but only something holy can be profaned. Violate says a line was crossed; profane says the line was sacred.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

honor: to treat with great respect

revere: to regard with deep awe and respect

Where it sits · how badly the holy is treated — disrespect → profane → desecrate

disrespect vs. profane: Disrespect is far milder and much broader than profane -- you can disrespect a teacher with an eye roll, while to profane something means treating what is held sacred as though it were worthless.

desecrate vs. profane: Desecrate is the most forceful word here: to profane a place is to treat it without the reverence it is owed, while to desecrate it suggests active violation, like smashing or defacing what people hold holy.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — pro-

prefix — pro-: before, in front of, outside (Latin)

root — -fane

root — -fane: temple, sacred place (Latin (fanum))

Put it together

Put it together: Latin profanus described whatever stood pro fano, 'outside the temple' -- ordinary, unconsecrated ground. To profane something is to drag it out of the temple and treat it as common, from the same root fanum that gives us fanatic, once a word for someone driven into a frenzy at a temple.

Use the root in a new word: fanatic

Use the root in a new word: fanatic: A lifelong fanatic, he has not missed a home game in thirty years.

Word Choice

This unit teaches profane as a verb: to profane a temple, a memorial, a ritual. You may also meet profane as an adjective meaning 'vulgar or blasphemous' ('profane language'), but that is a different use and not the one tested here.
